KEY MESSAGE 1...A plume of anomalous, and deep, moisture will 
get pulled north through the Southeastern U.S. in advance of a 
two cold fronts this weekend. The front will initially move 
through ENC on Saturday, then stall offshore before lifting back
north on Sunday. This will occur as a weak area of low pressure
rides NE along the front. As the low moves off the coast, it 
will drag the front back south through ENC later Sunday into 
Sunday night. 

Modest heating of a moist boundary layer should allow moderate 
instability to build ahead of the front today, especially 
across our southern counties south of HWY 70. It's there where 
we expect the greatest coverage of showers and thunderstorms to 
be focused this afternoon and evening. Guidance differ some on 
the progression of the front on Saturday, but with strong 
ridging centered offshore, it stands to reason that the progress
of the front will be slowed, favoring a frontal passage during 
peak heating for our southern counties. Moderate instability 
plus PWATs AoA climo maximums for early October, suggests a 
risk of high rainfall rates at times. Ensemble guidance suggests
0.50-1.50" of rain, on average, in this area. However, where 
convection is the most persistent, rainfall totals may reach as 
high as 2-3". This may support a risk of urban and poor drainage
flooding. 3-hr flash flood guidance is 3-4" in this area, which
suggests the risk of flash flooding is low based on the 
potential higher- end amounts being below FFG. It's worth 
watching, though, given such high moisture content. As such, WPC
has included this area, where the seabreeze and front will meet
this afternoon, in a Slight Risk of Excessive Rainfall.

On Sunday, guidance differs on how far north the front will get
as it briefly lifts back as a warm front. This doesn't appear 
to impact the ENC from a coverage standpoint. However, if the 
front were to lift further north, it could open up the potential
for more instability to be available while the FA is warm
sectored, which could support higher rainfall rates and 
amounts. This could also have an impact on temperatures. 
Regardless, increased low- mid level convergence interacting 
with a very moist airmass should lead to a widespread area of 
showers and isolated thunderstorms. For the area at large, the 
greatest coverage of showers and thunderstorms is expected on 
Sunday.

In total, 1-3" of rain appears likely for much of ENC over the 
weekend, 2-4" over the area from Greenville S and W. The 
highest rainfall amounts expected in an area roughly outlining 
Duplin Co to New Bern to Newport/Havelock to Jacksonville, 
where there will be the potential for heavy rain both Saturday 
and Sunday (compared to just Sunday for the northeastern 
counties of ENC). Highly localized weekend totals of 4-6" aren't
out of the realm of possibility in this area.

The risk of severe thunderstorms continues to look low due to 
weak shear and weak mid-level lapse rates. However, perhaps a 
few water- loaded downdrafts of 30-40 mph will occur Saturday 
afternoon when instability is at its peak. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...In the wake of the weekend front, a stiff 
NEerly breeze will develop and peak MON night into TUE. This 
will lead to building seas and elevated water levels. 
Astronomical tide levels will luckily be on the way down, but 
seas building to 7ft, though relatively choppy periodicity of 7 
sec, but enough to lead to further beach and dune erosion 
concerns across the areas with severely diminished dune 
structures. Strongest winds of 20-25 kt with higher gusts 
expected MON night into TUE morning. Winds remain out of the 
N-NE into late- week, but speeds diminish to 10-15kt late TUE 
and beyond.
